title: A Letter from the Palace
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 31 of 40
content:
Zuko's letter arrived during the morning tea service, when Iroh had both hands full of cups.

The courier set the sealed packet on the counter and asked for a receipt. Mina looked at the Fire Nation crest, then at the customers waiting for their orders.

"I can sign for it," I offered.

"Please," Iroh said. "If I set these down, the jasmine will go bitter."

His voice was light. The way he watched the packet was not.

We finished the orders before opening it. An older customer wanted less hot water; another asked why the price of mountain tea had increased. Mina explained the supplier's shortage and offered the ordinary house blend. There was no royal decree that could change what the delivery cart carried.

Only after the last customer had gone did Iroh take the packet into the courtyard.

He sat beneath the climbing vine, opened the letter and read it twice.

"Zuko?" I asked.

He nodded.

"Is he well?"

"As well as anyone can be who discovers each morning that a throne is a very uncomfortable chair."

I smiled. "What does he want?"

"Advice."

"About?"

"A coastal warehouse once used for military stores. The port workers want space for cargo; displaced families want shelter. The merchants say they cannot operate if the building is taken from trade. Everyone has made an argument that is at least partly true."

"What does Zuko ask?"

Iroh read the last line aloud: "How do I know whether a difficult decision is right when everyone will be disappointed?"

I sat beside him.

"That's a hard question."

"I had hoped to provide an easy answer."

"Would an easy answer be honest?"

He folded the letter with unnecessary precision.

"No."

We stayed there for a while. Iroh watched a pair of birds argue over the courtyard wall. I could almost see the old general turning the warehouse into a map of competing forces: one side here, another there, a line that could be held.

"What do you know about the building?" I asked.

"Very little."

"Then what could you tell him without deciding for the people who live there?"

He considered.

"That the workers should be heard, and the families. That neither needs to be treated as a problem obstructing his wisdom."

"That's a start."

I took out my notebook and drew two columns. One held things Iroh had learned from mistakes. The other held questions only the people at the harbor could answer: the floor's condition, seasonal storms, who could safely use the building, what it would cost to maintain.

Iroh examined the columns.

"Are you writing a report on my ignorance?"

"A very affectionate report."

"With dreadful handwriting."

"That too."

He laughed, then grew quiet.

"I miss him," he said.

"Zuko?"

"Yes. I miss being close enough to see when he has gone without sleep. But I do not miss the palace, the way every kindness becomes an obligation someone can invoke later."

"Would you like to visit?"

"Sometimes. Not as a minister who never returns home."

"Then say that."

He looked at me.

"Can one write to a Fire Lord and offer help without offering one's entire life?"

"Apparently we're about to find out."

He reached for the pen.

I stopped him gently.

"Before you write, can we talk about tonight?"

He frowned. "What about tonight?"

"We planned dinner together. You've been postponing sleep whenever a letter from the palace arrives. I'm not asking you to ignore Zuko. I'm asking whether you'd like to answer him tomorrow instead."

The expression on his face was almost painful.

"He needs me."

"I know. And he also needs to know that he can choose something with the people he's responsible for. You can't live every day on both sides of the world."

Iroh watched the seal.

"You make an old man's usefulness sound very limited."

"No. I make it sound like a choice."

Iroh opened a fresh sheet and began his reply to Zuko, then stopped.

"I was going to tell him what to do."

"Does he need an order?"

"No. He asked whether I could advise."

"Then perhaps write what you've learned and ask what he's already tried."

Iroh smiled faintly. "You make it sound so reasonable."

"It isn't easier. It just leaves him room to choose."

He wrote about the limits of what he knew from a distance. The old supply route in Zuko's letter had been damaged by bad weather, but Iroh couldn't honestly prescribe a repair based on a sketch and a few anxious lines. He could suggest who might examine it and offer to talk when Zuko wanted.

"I want him safe," he said.

"I know."

"Sometimes I remember being the man who could order an army, and I think I should be able to make one nephew safe."

I touched the edge of the paper. "You can love him without turning him into another command."

The words cost me something too. I'd caught myself hoping Iroh would be equally decisive about my own worries, that his wisdom would spare me the work of choosing. He wasn't a shelter I could simply move into and stop being responsible for my life.

He sealed the letter only after reading it through, then showed me the final line because he wanted to: *Tell me what you need, not what you think I expect you to need.*

I smiled.

"That sounds like a good question for the shop too."

He glanced at Mina through the open door. She was counting stock and pretending she hadn't been listening.

"She has been asking me that question for years," he said.

"And?"

"I am a slow student."

We laughed. He put the sealed letter with the courier's papers rather than holding it hostage until he felt less worried. The shop clock chimed the hour, and Iroh went to sign the delivery invoice he'd promised Mina before closing.

He sat back.

Mina appeared at the courtyard door with a delivery invoice. Two jars of citrus peel had been billed as three. Iroh glanced at the letter, then took the invoice.

"This I can solve before dinner," he said.

He asked Mina to compare the delivery sheet with the actual jars. They found the arithmetic error and drafted a note to the supplier. No magic, no bending, no palace messenger; just an ordinary business that would otherwise have paid for something it hadn't received.

Before closing, Iroh asked Mina whether she would prefer the late shift on Thursday.

"Why?" she asked.

"I have a date."

Mina looked at me, then back at him.

"That is not a reason to rearrange my week without asking."

"Precisely why I'm asking."

She checked the schedule and offered to trade one evening for a morning shift she wanted free. Iroh wrote down the exchange and confirmed her hours would remain paid.

"That is the most romantic thing I've heard from you all day," I said.

"Paying staff fairly?"

"Knowing their lives don't vanish because ours are busy."

Mina hid a smile as she put the ledger away.

Iroh looked at the table where Zuko's letter waited.

"That, too, is something I ought to remember when advising my nephew," he said.

By closing time Iroh seemed less tense.

He made dinner. We argued over how much ginger counted as an unreasonable amount.

"It is a philosophical matter," he told me.

"It is a question of whether the soup still tastes like soup."

"All philosophy begins with a bowl."

I laughed.

After we ate, he took a fresh sheet of paper.

"I would like to write a short answer," he said. "Would you sit nearby without correcting my every sentence?"

"That's going to require discipline."

"From both of us."

He began by telling Zuko he loved him. He suggested inviting the workers, families and merchants to explain their needs in their own words and checking the building before promising it to anyone. He offered to visit at an agreed time if his nephew wished.

He stopped before adding a fourth paragraph.

"Enough?" I asked.

"Probably."

I looked at the letter, then at him.

"We're getting better at knowing when to stop."

"On rare occasions."

We had already spoken openly about my being ethically non-monogamous and preferring polyamory. Iroh understood that loving him did not mean ending every other relationship. The same principle mattered here: I did not want him to have to abandon his nephew to belong with me, or abandon his own life to be a good uncle.

"May I kiss you?" I asked.

He smiled.

"I had rather hoped you would."

We kissed beneath the vine, slow and warm. When we drew apart he admitted the soup had contained too much ginger. I laughed against his cheek.

The letter rested on the table while we went upstairs. We closed the door and kept the rest of the night to ourselves.

In the morning he handed it to the courier without demanding a promise that Zuko would follow his advice.

Then he opened the shop on time.

Mina pointed at the stove.

"It still needs repair."

Iroh sighed.

"An enemy I know how to face."

I fetched the tools.
